title: Keep it to one page
tip: Especially for fresh grads and early-career roles - recruiters spend seconds per resume, and one page forces you to prioritize what actually matters.

title: Lead with Projects if your work history is thin
tip: Personal or academic projects often say more than a short work history. Include a live link or GitHub repo whenever you can - a working demo beats a description.

title: Quantify impact wherever possible
tip: "Improved page load time by 40%" beats "Worked on performance." Numbers make claims verifiable and memorable.

title: List technologies precisely
tip: Name the actual languages, frameworks, and tools you used - not vague phrases like "various technologies." Both recruiters and ATS scanners look for exact keywords.

title: Skip the generic objective paragraph
tip: Lines like "Motivated CS graduate seeking opportunities..." are filler that wastes your most valuable space. A tight one-line summary can work, but cut the fluff.

title: Order sections by relevance, not tradition
tip: For a fresh grad, Education and Projects usually belong near the top, not buried below a short or irrelevant work history.

title: Use a clean, ATS-friendly format
tip: Heavy graphics, tables, and multi-column layouts often break automated resume-screening software before a human ever sees your resume.

title: Tailor it per application
tip: Listing every language and tool you've ever touched reads as unfocused. Highlight what's actually relevant to the specific role you're applying for.

title: Proofread for consistency
tip: Same date format, same tense throughout (past tense for past roles, present for your current one), consistent punctuation. Small inconsistencies are an easy first filter for recruiters looking for a reason to reject.

title: Get someone else to review it
tip: A second pair of eyes catches typos and awkward phrasing you've read past a dozen times.
